claim: The retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) is proposed as a CO2 chemosensory nucleus mediating adaptive respiratory changes.
source: In the medulla oblongata, the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) and rostral medullary Raphe are proposed as CO2 chemosensory nuclei mediating adaptive respiratory changes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known hypothesis in the field.

claim: The rostral medullary Raphe is proposed as a CO2 chemosensory nucleus mediating adaptive respiratory changes.
source: In the medulla oblongata, the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) and rostral medullary Raphe are proposed as CO2 chemosensory nuclei mediating adaptive respiratory changes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known hypothesis in the field.

claim: Hypercapnia induces active expiration.
source: Hypercapnia also induces active expiration, an adaptive change thought to be controlled by the lateral parafacial region (pFL).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established observation.

claim: The lateral parafacial region (pFL) is thought to control active expiration during hypercapnia.
source: Hypercapnia also induces active expiration, an adaptive change thought to be controlled by the lateral parafacial region (pFL).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a hypothesis in the field.

claim: GCaMP6 expression and head-mounted mini-microscopes were used to image Ca2+ activity in the RTN, Raphe, and pFL in awake adult mice during hypercapnia.
source: Here, we use GCaMP6 expression and head-mounted mini-microscopes to image Ca2+ activity in these nuclei in awake adult mice during hypercapnia.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Activity in the pFL supports its role as a homogenous neuronal population that drives active expiration.
source: Activity in the pFL supports its role as a homogenous neuronal population that drives active expiration.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: Chemosensory responses in the RTN and Raphe differ in their temporal characteristics.
source: Our data show that chemosensory responses in the RTN and Raphe differ in their temporal characteristics and sensitivity to CO2, raising the possibility these nuclei act in a coordinated way to generate adaptive ventilatory responses to hypercapnia.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract based on the study's data.

claim: Chemosensory responses in the RTN and Raphe differ in their sensitivity to CO2.
source: Our data show that chemosensory responses in the RTN and Raphe differ in their temporal characteristics and sensitivity to CO2, raising the possibility these nuclei act in a coordinated way to generate adaptive ventilatory responses to hypercapnia.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract based on the study's data.

claim: The RTN and Raphe may act in a coordinated way to generate adaptive ventilatory responses to hypercapnia.
source: Our data show that chemosensory responses in the RTN and Raphe differ in their temporal characteristics and sensitivity to CO2, raising the possibility these nuclei act in a coordinated way to generate adaptive ventilatory responses to hypercapnia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Breathing fulfills two essential functions: provision of oxygen to support metabolism and removal of the metabolic by-product CO2.
source: Breathing fulfils two essential functions: provision of oxygen to support metabolism; and removal of the metabolic by-product, CO2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Over-accumulation of CO2 in blood will result in death from the consequent drop in pH.
source: Rapid and regulated removal of CO2 is essential because its over-accumulation in blood will result in death from the consequent drop in pH.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The primacy of the ventral medulla surface (VMS) in central chemoreception was described almost 60 years ago.
source: Whilst the primacy of the ventral medulla surface (VMS) in central chemoreception was described almost 60 years ago, this region contains multiple chemosensory nuclei that are candidates to mediate adaptive control of breathing (Nattie and Li, 1994; Richerson, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as historical knowledge with citations.

claim: The ventral medulla surface contains multiple chemosensory nuclei that are candidates to mediate adaptive control of breathing.
source: Whilst the primacy of the ventral medulla surface (VMS) in central chemoreception was described almost 60 years ago, this region contains multiple chemosensory nuclei that are candidates to mediate adaptive control of breathing (Nattie and Li, 1994; Richerson, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Central chemosensitivity is mediated by a network of chemosensory nuclei distributed throughout the brainstem and extending as far as the limbic system.
source: This has led to the idea that central chemosensitivity is mediated by a network of chemosensory nuclei distributed throughout the brainstem and extending as far as the limbic system (Huckstepp and Dale, 2011b).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the field with a supporting citation.

claim: There are multiple phenotypes of neurons within single chemosensory nuclei.
source: Furthermore, there are multiple phenotypes of neurons within single chemosensory nuclei (Huckstepp et al., 2018; Iceman et al., 2014; Iceman and Harris, 2014; Johansen et al., 2015), and even within previously well-defined subpopulations of neurons (Shi et al., 2017; Stornetta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Brain imaging techniques have been developed to allow recording of activity of defined cell populations in awake, freely moving animals even in deep brain structures such as the hypothalamus.
source: Recently, brain imaging techniques have been developed to allow recording of activity of defined cell populations in awake, freely moving animals even in deep brain structures such as the hypothalamus (Ziv and Ghosh, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as recent technological development with a supporting citation.

claim: The imaging methods require expression of genetically encoded Ca2+ indicators such as GCaMP6 in the relevant neurons.
source: These methods require: the expression of genetically encoded Ca2+ indicators such as GCaMP6 in the relevant neurons; the implantation of gradient refractive index (GRIN) lenses at the correct stereotaxic position; and a head-mounted mini-epifluorescence microscope to enable image acquisition during the free behaviour of the mouse.
evidence: This describes the technical requirements of the imaging method.

claim: The imaging methods require implantation of gradient refractive index (GRIN) lenses at the correct stereotaxic position.
source: These methods require: the expression of genetically encoded Ca2+ indicators such as GCaMP6 in the relevant neurons; the implantation of gradient refractive index (GRIN) lenses at the correct stereotaxic position; and a head-mounted mini-epifluorescence microscope to enable image acquisition during the free behaviour of the mouse.
evidence: This describes the technical requirements of the imaging method.

claim: The imaging methods require a head-mounted mini-epifluorescence microscope to enable image acquisition during the free behaviour of the mouse.
source: These methods require: the expression of genetically encoded Ca2+ indicators such as GCaMP6 in the relevant neurons; the implantation of gradient refractive index (GRIN) lenses at the correct stereotaxic position; and a head-mounted mini-epifluorescence microscope to enable image acquisition during the free behaviour of the mouse.
evidence: This describes the technical requirements of the imaging method.

claim: Evidence strongly favours the involvement of the RTN in the central chemosensory response.
source: In this paper, we study the activity of neurons in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) (Mulkey et al., 2004; Nattie and Li, 1994; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011) and the rostral medullary raphe (Bradley et al., 2002; Ray et al., 2011; Richerson, 1995). Evidence strongly favours their involvement in the central chemosensory response, but thorough understanding as to how these nuclei contribute to central chemosensitivity has been hampered by the inability to record the activity of their constituent cells in awake freely behaving adult rodents.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Evidence strongly favours the involvement of the rostral medullary raphe in the central chemosensory response.
source: In this paper, we study the activity of neurons in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) (Mulkey et al., 2004; Nattie and Li, 1994; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011) and the rostral medullary raphe (Bradley et al., 2002; Ray et al., 2011; Richerson, 1995). Evidence strongly favours their involvement in the central chemosensory response, but thorough understanding as to how these nuclei contribute to central chemosensitivity has been hampered by the inability to record the activity of their constituent cells in awake freely behaving adult rodents.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Understanding of how the RTN and Raphe contribute to central chemosensitivity has been hampered by the inability to record the activity of their constituent cells in awake freely behaving adult rodents.
source: Evidence strongly favours their involvement in the central chemosensory response, but thorough understanding as to how these nuclei contribute to central chemosensitivity has been hampered by the inability to record the activity of their constituent cells in awake freely behaving adult rodents.

claim: Neuronal recordings have been made from young (<14 d) or adult rodents under anaesthesia.
source: Instead, neuronal recordings have been made from young (<14 d) or adult rodents under anaesthesia.
evidence: This describes the prior state of the field.

claim: The chemosensory control of breathing matures postnatally.
source: Both of these methods have significant drawbacks -the chemosensory control of breathing matures postnatally; and anaesthesia is known to depress the activity of respiratory neurons and reconfigure the circuit.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about respiratory development.

claim: Anaesthesia is known to depress the activity of respiratory neurons and reconfigure the circuit.
source: Both of these methods have significant drawbacks -the chemosensory control of breathing matures postnatally; and anaesthesia is known to depress the activity of respiratory neurons and reconfigure the circuit.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the effects of anaesthesia.

claim: During resting eupneic breathing, there is little active expiration.
source: During resting eupneic breathing, there is little active expiration instead the expiratory step involves elastic rebound of the respiratory muscles to push air out of the lungs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about normal breathing.

claim: During resting eupneic breathing, the expiratory step involves elastic rebound of the respiratory muscles to push air out of the lungs.
source: During resting eupneic breathing, there is little active expiration instead the expiratory step involves elastic rebound of the respiratory muscles to push air out of the lungs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about normal breathing mechanics.

claim: When the intensity of breathing is increased during exercise or hypercapnia, active expiration occurs.
source: However, when the intensity of breathing is increased for example during exercise or hypercapnia, active expiration (recruitment of abdominal muscles to push air out of the lungs) occurs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about breathing during increased demand.

claim: Active expiration involves recruitment of abdominal muscles to push air out of the lungs.
source: However, when the intensity of breathing is increased for example during exercise or hypercapnia, active expiration (recruitment of abdominal muscles to push air out of the lungs) occurs.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: Mounting evidence suggests the pFL may contain the expiratory oscillator.
source: Mounting evidence suggests the pFL may contain the expiratory oscillator and that neurons in this nucleus are recruited to evoke active expiration (Huckstepp et al., 2015; Huckstepp et al., 2016; Pagliardini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in the pFL are recruited to evoke active expiration.
source: Mounting evidence suggests the pFL may contain the expiratory oscillator and that neurons in this nucleus are recruited to evoke active expiration (Huckstepp et al., 2015; Huckstepp et al., 2016; Pagliardini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The pFL did not undergo sustained activation during hypercapnia.
source: Our data show the pFL did not undergo sustained activation during hypercapnia, but instead contributed to acute transient high amplitude expiratory events.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the introduction.

claim: The pFL contributed to acute transient high amplitude expiratory events during hypercapnia.
source: Our data show the pFL did not undergo sustained activation during hypercapnia, but instead contributed to acute transient high amplitude expiratory events.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the introduction.

claim: Many RTN neurons exhibited fast adapting responses to hypercapnia.
source: We found that neurons in the RTN and Raphe exhibited a range of responses to hypercapnia. Many RTN neurons exhibited fast adapting responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the introduction.

claim: Fast adapting responses were less common in the Raphe than in the RTN.
source: This response type was less common in the Raphe, and many Raphe neurons exhibited a slower graded response.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the introduction.

claim: Many Raphe neurons exhibited a slower graded response to hypercapnia.
source: This response type was less common in the Raphe, and many Raphe neurons exhibited a slower graded response.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the introduction.

claim: The data are consistent with a tiered chemosensory network, with the RTN and Raphe responsible for detecting different aspects of the hypercapnic stimulus.
source: Our data are consistent with a tiered chemosensory network, with the RTN and Raphe responsible for detecting different aspects of the hypercapnic stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings stated in the introduction.

claim: The GRIN lens has a diameter of 600 µm with a focal plane ~300 µm below the lens.
source: The GRIN lens has a diameter of 600 µm with a focal plane ~300 µm below the lens (Jennings et al., 2015; Resendez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a technical specification with supporting citations.

claim: The focal plane varies depending upon the distance between the camera and GRIN lens.
source: However, the focal plane varies depending upon the distance between the camera and GRIN lens, which can be altered via a manual turret adjustment to optimise the focus on fluorescent cells.
evidence: This describes a technical property of the imaging system.

claim: The focal depth was 100 µm at any single turret setting.
source: The focal depth (in which the beads were sharply focussed) was 100 µm at any single setting and the full focal plane ranged from 150 to 450 µm below the end of the lens as the turret moved from its lowest to highest setting.
evidence: This is a measurement from the calibration experiment described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The full focal plane ranged from 150 to 450 µm below the end of the lens as the turret moved from its lowest to highest setting.
source: The focal depth (in which the beads were sharply focussed) was 100 µm at any single setting and the full focal plane ranged from 150 to 450 µm below the end of the lens as the turret moved from its lowest to highest setting.
evidence: This is a measurement from the calibration experiment described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Data from 18 mice comprising recordings from 194 cells were included for analysis.
source: Following assessment for inclusion/exclusion criteria, data from 18 mice comprising recordings from 194 cells were included for analysis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the sample size of the study as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Transduction of RTN neurons with AAV-syn-GFP (not Ca2+ sensitive) did not produce large increases in fluorescence during hypercapnia.
source: We transduced RTN neurons of three mice with AAV-syn-GFP and performed imaging during a hypercapnic challenge (Figure 1C–D, Figure 1—video 1). This allowed measurement of comparable levels of fluorescence to GCaMP6 to determine whether movement by itself, in the absence of any Ca2+ reporter activity, could generate confounding fluorescent signals. Analysis of changes in fluorescence showed only small amplitude (often negative-going) fluctuations. In no case did we observe large increases in fluorescence of the type we routinely observed when GCaMP6 was expressed (e.g. Figure 1E), suggesting that movement per se cannot give fluorescence signals that resemble Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This is a control experiment described in the text and shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Movement per se cannot give fluorescence signals that resemble Ca2+ signals.
source: In no case did we observe large increases in fluorescence of the type we routinely observed when GCaMP6 was expressed (e.g. Figure 1E), suggesting that movement per se cannot give fluorescence signals that resemble Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the GFP control experiment.

claim: Large movements of the head/body did not evoke noticeable changes in GCaMP6 fluorescence.
source: When we examined the GCaMP6 fluorescence in conjunction with the sonograms of head and body movement, we observed that: (i) large movements of the head/body did not evoke noticeable changes in GCaMP6 fluorescence (Figure 1Ea,b); (ii) GCaMP6 Ca2+ signals characterized by a fast rise and exponential decay occurred in the absence of any movement (Figure 1Ec,f); and (iii) similar shaped Ca2+ signals occurred during movement (Figure 1Ed,e).
evidence: This is an observation from the movement analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: GCaMP6 Ca2+ signals characterized by a fast rise and exponential decay occurred in the absence of any movement.
source: When we examined the GCaMP6 fluorescence in conjunction with the sonograms of head and body movement, we observed that: (i) large movements of the head/body did not evoke noticeable changes in GCaMP6 fluorescence (Figure 1Ea,b); (ii) GCaMP6 Ca2+ signals characterized by a fast rise and exponential decay occurred in the absence of any movement (Figure 1Ec,f); and (iii) similar shaped Ca2+ signals occurred during movement (Figure 1Ed,e).
evidence: This is an observation from the movement analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Similar shaped Ca2+ signals occurred during movement.
source: When we examined the GCaMP6 fluorescence in conjunction with the sonograms of head and body movement, we observed that: (i) large movements of the head/body did not evoke noticeable changes in GCaMP6 fluorescence (Figure 1Ea,b); (ii) GCaMP6 Ca2+ signals characterized by a fast rise and exponential decay occurred in the absence of any movement (Figure 1Ec,f); and (iii) similar shaped Ca2+ signals occurred during movement (Figure 1Ed,e).
evidence: This is an observation from the movement analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Movement of the head or body of the animal does not prevent the recording of genuine changes in GCaMP6 fluorescence related to changes in intracellular Ca2+.
source: Together this suggests that movement of the head or body of the animal does not prevent the recording of genuine changes in GCaMP6 fluorescence related to changes in intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the movement analysis.

claim: Intraperitoneal kainic acid injection induced electrographic seizures in anaesthetized mice.
source: To elicit neural activity, we induced electrographic seizures via intraperitoneal kainic acid injection in mice in the absence of any behavioural seizure movements such as partial (including forelimb or hindlimb) or whole body continuous clonic seizures (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This describes an experimental manipulation shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: After ~70 min of kainic acid injection, perturbations of the WBP trace and correlated Ca2+ activity in the RTN neurons occurred.
source: After ~70 min this resulted in perturbations of the WBP trace and correlated Ca2+ activity in the RTN neurons, presumably denoting the invasion of seizures into this nucleus.
evidence: This is an observation from the seizure experiment shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The fluorescence changes during seizures were of two types: transients with a fast rise and exponential fall, and slower sustained changes.
source: Detailed examination revealed that the fluorescence changes were of two types: (i) transients with a fast rise and exponential fall; and (ii) slower sustained changes (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an observation from the seizure experiment shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Two types of genuine Ca2+ signal are expected in recordings from freely-moving mice: fast transients with an exponential decay phase, and slower more gradual rises.
source: This is an important observation as it shows that we expect to see two types of genuine Ca2+ signal in recordings from freely-moving mice: fast transients with an exponential decay phase, that may sum together and slower more gradual rises.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the seizure experiment.

claim: 144 out of 194 cells were eligible for study after applying inclusion criteria.
source: Applying these criteria left 144/194 cells eligible for study.
evidence: This describes the final sample size after quality control.

claim: Inhibited (I) neurons displayed spontaneous Ca2+ activity at rest, which was greatly reduced during both 3 and 6% inspired CO2.
source: Inhibited (I) Displayed spontaneous Ca2+ activity at rest, which was greatly reduced during both 3 and 6% inspired CO2 and could exhibit rebound activity following the end of the hypercapnic episode.
evidence: This is a definition of a neuronal response category based on observed data.

claim: Excited - adapting (EA) neurons were silent or with low level activity at rest and showed the greatest Ca2+ activity in response to a change in 3% inspired CO2.
source: Excited - adapting (EA) Silent or with low level activity at rest and showed the greatest Ca2+ activity in response to a change in 3% inspired CO2. Following an initial burst of activity, they were either silent or displayed lower level activity throughout the remainder of the hypercapnic episode.
evidence: This is a definition of a neuronal response category based on observed data.

claim: EA neurons essentially encoded the beginning and end of hypercapnia.
source: These cells essentially encoded the beginning and end of hypercapnia.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EA neuronal response pattern.

claim: Excited - graded (EG) neurons were silent or with low level activity at rest and displayed an increase in Ca2+ activity at 3% inspired CO2 with a further increase in activity at 6%.
source: Excited - graded (EG) Silent or with low level activity at rest and displayed an increase in Ca2+ activity at 3% inspired CO2 with a further increase in activity at 6% that returned to baseline upon removal of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a definition of a neuronal response category based on observed data.

claim: EG neurons encoded the level of inspired CO2.
source: These cells encoded the level of inspired CO2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EG neuronal response pattern.

claim: Tonic (T) neurons displayed spontaneous Ca2+ activity throughout the recording that was unaffected by the hypercapnic episode.
source: Tonic (T) Displaying spontaneous Ca2+ activity throughout the recording that was unaffected by the hypercapnic episode but could provide tonic drive to the respiratory network.
evidence: This is a definition of a neuronal response category based on observed data.

claim: Sniff-coding (Sn) neurons displayed elevated Ca2+ signals correlated with exploratory sniffing.
source: Sniff-coding (Sn) Displayed elevated Ca2+ signals correlated with exploratory sniffing.
evidence: This is a definition of a neuronal response category based on observed data.

claim: Expiratory (Exp) neurons displayed elevated Ca2+ signals correlated with large expiratory events.
source: Expiratory (Exp) Displayed elevated Ca2+ signals correlated with large expiratory events.
evidence: This is a definition of a neuronal response category based on observed data.

claim: Non-coding (NC) neurons displayed low frequency or sporadic Ca2+ activity that was neither tonic in nature nor had any discernable activity that related to the hypercapnic stimulus or any respiratory event.
source: Non-coding (NC) Displayed low frequency or sporadic Ca2+ activity that was neither tonic in nature nor had any discernable activity that related to the hypercapnic stimulus or any respiratory event.
evidence: This is a definition of a neuronal response category based on observed data.

claim: Non-coding respiratory related (NC-RR) neurons displayed Ca2+ activity that did not code the hypercapnic stimulus, but was related to variability in breathing frequency.
source: Non-coding respiratory related (NC-RR) Displayed Ca2+ activity that did not code the hypercapnic stimulus, but it was instead related to variability in breathing frequency.
evidence: This is a definition of a neuronal response category based on observed data.

claim: EA neurons cluster below the line of identity (x=y) in a plot of 6% CO2 response versus 3% CO2 response.
source: EA neurons as they showed more activity at 3% compared to 6% CO2 should cluster below the line of identity (x=y), whereas EG neurons as they respond more strongly to 6% than 3% should cluster above the line of identity.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the definition of EA neurons, confirmed by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: EG neurons cluster above the line of identity (x=y) in a plot of 6% CO2 response versus 3% CO2 response.
source: EA neurons as they showed more activity at 3% compared to 6% CO2 should cluster below the line of identity (x=y), whereas EG neurons as they respond more strongly to 6% than 3% should cluster above the line of identity.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the definition of EG neurons, confirmed by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: NC neurons cluster around the origin (x=y=0) in a plot of 6% CO2 response versus 3% CO2 response.
source: NC neurons as they did not show a response to hypercapnia should be clustered around the origin (x=y=0), and the I neurons should be clustered in the quadrant where the change in Ca2+ activity to both stimuli is negative.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the definition of NC neurons, confirmed by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: I neurons cluster in the quadrant where the change in Ca2+ activity to both stimuli is negative.
source: NC neurons as they did not show a response to hypercapnia should be clustered around the origin (x=y=0), and the I neurons should be clustered in the quadrant where the change in Ca2+ activity to both stimuli is negative.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the definition of I neurons, confirmed by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: ~7% (9/132) of transduced neurons in the focal plane of the microscope co-labelled with ChAT.
source: The localization of successful and accurate transduction was confirmed posthoc by using choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) staining to define the facial nucleus and the location of the transduced cells (Figure 2B), with ~7% (9/132) of transduced neurons in the focal plane of the microscope co-labelled with ChAT (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The lens track terminated under the caudal pole of the facial nucleus.
source: The lens track terminated under the caudal pole of the facial nucleus, containing the highest number of neurons (Figure 2B), with the focal plane 150–450 µm below that, covering the dorso-ventral extent of the RTN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of the lens as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The focal plane was 150–450 µm below the lens track, covering the dorso-ventral extent of the RTN.
source: The lens track terminated under the caudal pole of the facial nucleus, containing the highest number of neurons (Figure 2B), with the focal plane 150–450 µm below that, covering the dorso-ventral extent of the RTN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the anatomical coverage of the imaging as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2B.

claim: 43% (40/93) of NMB+ cells in the RTN were also transduced with GCaMP6.
source: We found 43% (40/93) of NMB + cells in the RTN were also transduced with GCaMP6, and 20% (40/204) of GCaMP + neurons in the RTN were NMB+.
evidence: This is a quantification from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2E.

claim: 20% (40/204) of GCaMP+ neurons in the RTN were NMB+.
source: We found 43% (40/93) of NMB + cells in the RTN were also transduced with GCaMP6, and 20% (40/204) of GCaMP + neurons in the RTN were NMB+.
evidence: This is a quantification from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2E.

claim: Ca2+ activity traces from 98 RTN neurons in 9 mice were retained after quality assessment.
source: After assessing the quality of recordings, we retained Ca2+ activity traces from 98 RTN neurons in 9 mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the final sample size for RTN neurons as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 4 out of 98 RTN neurons exhibited a graded response to hypercapnia (EG).
source: While we observed 4/98 neurons exhibited a graded response to hypercapnia (EG, Figure 2F and G, Figure 2—video 1), a much greater number (27/98) were of the adapting subtype (EA, Figure 2H1, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the RTN dataset.

claim: 27 out of 98 RTN neurons were of the adapting subtype (EA).
source: While we observed 4/98 neurons exhibited a graded response to hypercapnia (EG, Figure 2F and G, Figure 2—video 1), a much greater number (27/98) were of the adapting subtype (EA, Figure 2H1, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the RTN dataset.

claim: The adapting response in EA neurons matched the time course of changes in VE calculated from the WBP records.
source: This adapting response may also be physiologically meaningful, as it matched the time course of changes in VE calculated from the WBP records (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In three mice, the averaged Ca2+ trace of the EA neurons matched the changes in VT for the same mouse.
source: In three mice the averaged Ca2+ trace of the EA neurons in each mouse matched the changes in VT for the same mouse and a plot of VT versus F/F0 for the Ca2+ signal gave a positive correlation (Figure 2J, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: A plot of VT versus F/F0 for the Ca2+ signal in EA neurons gave a positive correlation.
source: In three mice the averaged Ca2+ trace of the EA neurons in each mouse matched the changes in VT for the same mouse and a plot of VT versus F/F0 for the Ca2+ signal gave a positive correlation (Figure 2J, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The rates of Ca2+ sequestration did not greatly increase during hypercapnia in EA neurons.
source: An alternative explanation that the rates of Ca2+ sequestration greatly increased during hypercapnia such that Ca2+ levels fell even although firing rates increased can be excluded by examining the dynamics of individual Ca2+ transients. The rise time of these transients reflects the rate of Ca2+ influx, and the exponentially falling decay phase the rate of Ca2+ extrusion or sequestration. Comparison of these transients before, during and after the hypercapnic stimulus shows that these transients do not change in shape (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion from analysis of Ca2+ transient dynamics shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: 5 out of 98 RTN neurons were inhibited during hypercapnia.
source: A further 5/98 neurons were inhibited during hypercapnia (Figure 3A and C, blue traces and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the RTN dataset.

claim: 3 out of 98 RTN neurons were sniff-coding (Sn) neurons.
source: We recorded from sniff-coding (Sn) neurons, 3/98, which showed elevated Ca2+ signals correlated with sniffing (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the RTN dataset.

claim: In sniff-coding neurons, Ca2+ activity coincided with perturbations of the plethysmography traces.
source: In sniff-coding neurons, Ca2+ activity coincided with perturbations of the plethysmography traces (increase in respiratory frequency, increase of tidal volume, presence of expiration, Figure 3B and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Activity in sniff-coding neurons preceded the sniff by 0.4–0.8 s on average.
source: Analysis of the onset of the Ca2+ signal relative to the start of the sniff, showed that, on average, activity in these neurons preceded the sniff by 0.4–0.8 s (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantification from the timing analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 5 out of 98 RTN neurons were tonically active but did not encode any information about hypercapnia (T).
source: Additionally, 5/98 neurons which were tonically active but did not encode any information about hypercapnia (T, Figure 4A, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the RTN dataset.

claim: 35 out of 98 RTN neurons showed sporadic activity that did not correlate with CO2 (NC).
source: Of 98 neurons, 35 showed sporadic activity that did not correlate with CO2 (NC, Figure 4B) and a further 19/98 neurons that did not encode CO2 levels but displayed Ca2+ signals that were correlated to changes in respiratory frequency and were generally silent when tidal volume was at its greatest (NC-RR, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the RTN dataset.

claim: 19 out of 98 RTN neurons did not encode CO2 levels but displayed Ca2+ signals that were correlated to changes in respiratory frequency (NC-RR).
source: Of 98 neurons, 35 showed sporadic activity that did not correlate with CO2 (NC, Figure 4B) and a further 19/98 neurons that did not encode CO2 levels but displayed Ca2+ signals that were correlated to changes in respiratory frequency and were generally silent when tidal volume was at its greatest (NC-RR, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the RTN dataset.

claim: ~40% (39/98) of RTN neurons had activity patterns that were in some way modulated by CO2.
source: In summary for RTN neurons: ~40% (39/98) had activity patterns that were in some way modulated by CO2.
evidence: This is a summary quantification of CO2-responsive RTN neurons.

claim: 69% (27/39) of CO2-modulated RTN neurons displayed an adaptive response to CO2.
source: The majority of these neurons, 69% (27/39), displayed an adaptive response to CO2, thus marking the onset of hypercapnia.
evidence: This is a summary quantification of EA neurons among CO2-responsive RTN neurons.

claim: 10% (4/39) of CO2-modulated RTN neurons encoded the magnitude of hypercapnia.
source: Only a minority of neurons, 10% (4/39), encoded the magnitude of hypercapnia and a similar minority (13%; 5/39) were active and inhibited throughout the hypercapnic episode.
evidence: This is a summary quantification of EG neurons among CO2-responsive RTN neurons.

claim: 13% (5/39) of CO2-modulated RTN neurons were active and inhibited throughout the hypercapnic episode.
source: Only a minority of neurons, 10% (4/39), encoded the magnitude of hypercapnia and a similar minority (13%; 5/39) were active and inhibited throughout the hypercapnic episode.
evidence: This is a summary quantification of I neurons among CO2-responsive RTN neurons.

claim: Urethane anaesthesia had a deeply suppressive effect on the spontaneous activity of all RTN neurons.
source: As might be expected, compared to the awake state, urethane anaesthesia had a deeply suppressive effect on the spontaneous activity of all RTN neurons.
evidence: This is an observation from the anaesthesia comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under urethane anaesthesia, there was hardly any spontaneous activity in RTN neurons.
source: Whereas almost all neurons displayed spontaneous activity, there was hardly any activity under anaesthesia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is an observation from the anaesthesia comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The responses to hypercapnia in RTN neurons were greatly blunted under anaesthesia.
source: Furthermore, the responses to hypercapnia were greatly blunted, with many neurons simply being unresponsive.
evidence: This is an observation from the anaesthesia comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Responses to hypercapnia in RTN neurons differed between awake and anesthetised states.
source: When we examined those neurons that retained a chemosensory response to hypercapnia in the anesthetised state, these responses differed from those that the same neurons showed in the awake state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the anaesthesia comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 50% (57/113) of transduced neurons in the Raphe focal plane were TPH+ when using synapsin promoter.
source: Assessing the ability of this construct to transduce serotonergic neurons in this nucleus, we found that 57/113 (50%) of the transduced neurons in the focal plane of the microscope were TPH+ (tryptophan hydroxylase; a marker of serotonergic neurons) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5D.

claim: All neurons in the optical pathway of the microscope which expressed GCaMP6s driven by SERT promoter co-localised with TPH.
source: Post-hoc immunocytochemistry showed that all neurons in the optical pathway of the microscope (Figure 5E) which expressed GCaMP6s co-localised with TPH.
evidence: This is a quantification from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 9 synapsin GCaMP6s neurons and 17 SERT GCaMP6s neurons were recorded from the Raphe.
source: We recorded 9 synapsin GCaMP6s neurons and 17 SERT GCaMP6s neurons.
evidence: This describes the sample size for Raphe neurons.

claim: 8 out of 26 Raphe neurons exhibited a graded response to CO2 (EG).
source: A frequently observed class of neurons (8/26) exhibited a graded response to CO2 (EG, Figure 5G and H and Figure 5—video 1, synapsin).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the Raphe dataset.

claim: 4 out of 26 Raphe neurons showed the adapting response (EA).
source: 4/26 neurons showed the adapting response (EA, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the Raphe dataset.

claim: 10 out of 26 Raphe neurons were inhibited by CO2.
source: The commonest class of neurons in our dataset was inhibited by CO2 (10/26, all from mice transduced with GCaMP under the SERT promoter, Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—video 1 SERT).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the Raphe dataset.

claim: All 10 CO2-inhibited Raphe neurons were from mice transduced with GCaMP under the SERT promoter.
source: The commonest class of neurons in our dataset was inhibited by CO2 (10/26, all from mice transduced with GCaMP under the SERT promoter, Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—video 1 SERT).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the Raphe dataset.

claim: 4 out of 26 Raphe neurons displayed activity that was unaffected by hypercapnia (NC).
source: The remaining 4/26 neurons displayed activity that was unaffected by hypercapnia (NC, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a quantification of neuronal response types from the Raphe dataset.

claim: 85% (22/26) of Raphe neurons had Ca2+ activity patterns that were modulated by CO2.
source: In summary, 85% (22/26) of Raphe neurons had Ca2+ activity patterns that were modulated by CO2.
evidence: This is a summary quantification of CO2-responsive Raphe neurons.

claim: EA neurons were much less prevalent in the Raphe (15%) compared to the RTN.
source: Interestingly, unlike the RTN which showed considerable bias toward the EA functional type, EA neurons were much less prevalent in the Raphe (only 15%), with EG (31%), and I (38%) being the most common types of response we observed.
evidence: This is a summary comparison of neuronal response types between RTN and Raphe.

claim: EG (31%) and I (38%) were the most common types of response observed in the Raphe.
source: Interestingly, unlike the RTN which showed considerable bias toward the EA functional type, EA neurons were much less prevalent in the Raphe (only 15%), with EG (31%), and I (38%) being the most common types of response we observed.
evidence: This is a summary quantification of neuronal response types in the Raphe.

claim: There were no tonically active neurons in the Raphe.
source: In the Raphe, there were no tonically active neurons or neurons that were co-active with any non-respiratory related orofacial movements such as sniffing.
evidence: This is a summary observation about the Raphe dataset.

claim: There were no neurons in the Raphe that were co-active with sniffing.
source: In the Raphe, there were no tonically active neurons or neurons that were co-active with any non-respiratory related orofacial movements such as sniffing.
evidence: This is a summary observation about the Raphe dataset.

claim: The pFL is thought to be a subsidiary conditional oscillator for expiration that is normally suppressed at rest.
source: The pFL is thought to be a subsidiary conditional oscillator for expiration that is normally suppressed at rest (Huckstepp et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the field with a supporting citation.

claim: A hypercapnic stimulus causes an increase in respiratory frequency, tidal volume and the onset of active expiration.
source: A hypercapnic stimulus causes an increase in respiratory frequency, tidal volume and also the onset of active expiration (Huckstepp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: All pFL neurons showed the same discharge pattern.
source: That all pFL neurons showed the same discharge pattern, supports the hypothesis that the pFL is comprised of a single homogenous group of neurons acting with a single purpose (Huckstepp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the pFL dataset that supports a hypothesis.

claim: The pFL appears to be a simple on-off switch, rather than forming complex outputs.
source: Even though the nucleus appears to integrate information from many nuclei -RTN (Zoccal et al., 2018), C1, (Malheiros-Lima et al., 2020), NTS, rostral pedunculopontine tegmental (Silva et al., 2019) and the preBötC (Huckstepp et al., 2016) -the pFL appears to be a simple on-off switch, rather than forming complex outputs as we describe in the RTN.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pFL data.

claim: pFL neurons were only transiently active during large expiratory efforts.
source: Surprisingly, we found that pFL neurons were only transiently active during large expiratory efforts, (such as sniffing, sighing, or other forms of brief deep breathing), in contrast to the sustained active expiration previously reported (Huckstepp et al., 2015; Leirão et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the pFL dataset that differs from prior reports.

claim: Ca2+ activity in pFL neurons on average preceded an increase in tidal volume and respiratory frequency by ~0.4 s.
source: Whilst Ca2+ activity in the pFL neurons on average preceded an increase in tidal volume and respiratory frequency by ~0.4 s, some neurons showed Ca2+ activity only after changes in tidal volume and respiratory frequency had occurred (Figure 7H–J).
evidence: This is a quantification from the timing analysis shown in Figure 7H-J.

claim: Some pFL neurons showed Ca2+ activity only after changes in tidal volume and respiratory frequency had occurred.
source: Whilst Ca2+ activity in the pFL neurons on average preceded an increase in tidal volume and respiratory frequency by ~0.4 s, some neurons showed Ca2+ activity only after changes in tidal volume and respiratory frequency had occurred (Figure 7H–J).
evidence: This is an observation from the timing analysis shown in Figure 7H-J.

claim: The time separation between pFL activity and changes in tidal volume/respiratory frequency was independent of the level of inspired CO2.
source: This time separation was independent of the level of inspired CO2 (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: This is an observation from the timing analysis shown in Figure 7I-J.

claim: The timing characteristics of pFL neurons are more compatible with a correlative rather than a causal relationship between the activation of pFL neurons and changes in tidal volume and respiratory frequency.
source: These characteristics are more compatible with a correlative rather than a causal relationship between the activation of pFL neurons and changes in tidal volume and respiratory frequency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing data.

claim: Ca2+ activity in pFL neurons always preceded a change in the expiratory activity.
source: When we specifically studied the incidence of active expiration, we found that Ca2+ activity in pFL neurons always preceded a change in the expiratory activity (Figure 7H–M).
evidence: This is an observation from the timing analysis shown in Figure 7H-M.

claim: At 6% inspired CO2, the time difference between pFL activity and active expiration was ~0.5 s.
source: At 6% inspired CO2 this time difference was ~0.5 s. (Figure 7K and L), while at 9% inspired CO2 the time interval shortened to ~0.3 s (Figure 7K and M).
evidence: This is a quantification from the timing analysis shown in Figure 7K-L.

claim: At 9% inspired CO2, the time interval between pFL activity and active expiration shortened to ~0.3 s.
source: At 6% inspired CO2 this time difference was ~0.5 s. (Figure 7K and L), while at 9% inspired CO2 the time interval shortened to ~0.3 s (Figure 7K and M).
evidence: This is a quantification from the timing analysis shown in Figure 7K-M.

claim: In all 20 pFL neurons that exhibited activity, this activity preceded active expiration.
source: In all 20 neurons in the pFL that exhibited activity, this activity preceded active expiration.
evidence: This is a summary observation from the pFL dataset.

claim: The timing of pFL activity relative to active expiration is consistent with a causal rather than a correlative link.
source: This timing is consistent with a causal rather than a correlative link between neuronal activity in the pFL and induction of active expiration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing data.

claim: 2 out of 71 (1.5%) pFL neurons co-localised with ChAT.
source: Post-hoc immunocytochemistry showed that a small population of neurons which expressed GCaMP6 co-localised with ChAT (2/71, 1.5%, Figure 7B and D) and were located in the focal plane of the microscope (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: The Ca2+ signal cannot tell us the precise firing rates or dynamics of the neuronal activity.
source: The summation and temporal variation of the signal will depend on the Ca2+ buffering/extrusion systems within the cell, the density and activation properties of Ca2+ permeable channels, and whether Ca2+ may additionally be released from intracellular stores. Therefore, this Ca2+ signal cannot tell us the precise firing rates or dynamics of the neuronal activity, and so is an imprecise proxy of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged in the discussion.

claim: Ca2+ activity of neurons is a widely used method to assess their electrical activity.
source: Despite this imperfection, Ca2+ activity of neurons is a widely used to assess their electrical activity (Chen et al., 2013; Dana et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The rates of Ca2+ influx and extrusion or sequestration do not change with the hypercapnic stimulus.
source: We verified that the rates of Ca2+ influx and extrusion or sequestration do not change with the hypercapnic stimulus by examining individual Ca2+ transients before, during and after hypercapnia to show that their rise times and decay rates remain unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a verification from analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GCaMP6s was used for recording from the RTN and Raphe as it is the most sensitive Ca2+ sensor.
source: We used GCaMP6s for recording from the RTN and Raphe as this is the most sensitive Ca2+ sensor and we did not expect to need to resolve rapidly changing Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This explains the choice of Ca2+ indicator.

claim: GCaMP6f was used for the pFL to attempt to document cycle by cycle changes in fluorescence.
source: For the pFL we used faster responding, but less sensitive, GCaMP6f to attempt to document cycle by cycle changes in fluorescence, but these were not resolved in the current experiments.
evidence: This explains the choice of Ca2+ indicator for pFL recordings.

claim: The majority of RTN neurons in the dataset were of the EA subtype.
source: Notably, our dataset of RTN chemosensitive neurons contained a preponderance of the EA subtype.
evidence: This is a summary observation from the RTN dataset.

claim: EA neuronal responses are potentially well suited to detect small increases of inspired CO2 outside the normal range.
source: The EA neuronal responses are potentially well suited to detect small increases of inspired CO2 outside the normal range that can occur during normal behavioural conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the EA neuronal function.

claim: Raphe neurons could take over from RTN neurons during more sustained episodes of hypercapnia.
source: In contrast, the Raphe neurons tended to be active during the entire CO2 stimulus and conceivably these neurons could take over from RTN neurons during more sustained episodes of hypercapnia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the complementary roles of RTN and Raphe.

claim: The chemosensory network may be arranged in a hierarchy with each layer conveying a unique range of CO2.
source: These data provide an intriguing possibility that the chemosensory network is arranged in a hierarchy with each layer conveying a unique range of CO2.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the overall findings.
